title: Precepts and dogmas, Scripture's inward efficacy, and divinity-marks read in the whole
pass_a_gloss:
Sense of the locked Latin across precepts, mysteries above reason, inward efficacy, and whole-book marks (XLIII through XLVI): Precepts and dogmas of sacred Scripture also do not lack their own light; they even have by far the greatest. For clearer appearance: note that those teachings are of two kinds. Scripture teaches and commands many things of which men by nature have some notice, yet very confused and wavering. But Scripture those more lucidly laid open, and taught fully and accurately. Of such sort are what Scripture hands down concerning God's nature and attributes, namely concerning God's essence eternal, immense, and immutable, and concerning his infinite power, wisdom, goodness, and also justice, concerning the world's creation and of all things which in it are, concerning God's providence by which all he conserves, rules, and administers: Likewise concerning man's office both toward God and toward the neighbor, such as that God above all is to be loved, all things unto his glory to be referred, himself carefully to be worshiped and invoked, in him to be trusted, and upon his care to be reclined. The neighbor also to be loved, to all good to be done, injuries to be borne, humbly of oneself to be thought, innermost thoughts and affections pure to be kept, and in one word nearly all and each precepts of the Christian life, which in every part pure and sincere ought to be, and from which ought to be absent all filth and luxury. Those certainly and like things the conscience's sense proves, reason confirms, and of them certain rudiments are discerned in the pagans' books. For some things concerning God, piety, and man's office not contemptible they hand down. But yet obscurely, sparingly, coldly, doubtfully, and with of very many errors' admixture. But Scripture those in clear light places, and fully and openly teaches: so that after to us its light has shone, we wonder that things so certain and undoubted only thinly, doubtfully and obscurely by most excellent minds had been seen and handed down. But when those most excellent minds those things, whose truth already we discern by Scripture's benefit, so jejune and obscurely handed down, but Scripture so fully and perspicuously; and yet the sacred writers by erudition or nature's gifts above other men did not excel, nay on the contrary most were of human sciences rude and unlearned, necessary it is that they by another than nature's light were led, and by God taught and inspired.

But besides those things of which men by nature a thin certain and fleeing cognition have, sacred Scripture many things teaches which reason surpass, nor can the human mind those grasp, nor of them has it certain arguments: Yet so well they cohere with those which the conscience's sense proves, and of which right reason is convinced, and to those prior so consentaneous are, and so congruently and aptly superstructed, that enough it appears they are not human inventions, but of divine wisdom mysteries. Such is for example the doctrine of our sins' expiation through Christ God's and man's death and offering made on the cross, which to agree most is discerned with God's justice and mercy. For in this manner God's justice was satisfied, while our sins in Christ were punished, and mercy's, while to us forgiven. And with this doctrine coheres that dogma so sublime and lofty concerning three divine persons in one essence. For unless God's Son were God, and equal to the Father, his sacrifice would not have been of infinite value, such as was required that by it our sins be expiated, inasmuch as infinite punishment they had deserved. And such also the doctrine of the dead's resurrection. For it seems to be to reason consentaneous that a man who in the body well or ill acts, in the body also punishment or reward should receive of things justly or unjustly done: which since in this life it does not happen, to God's justice it agrees that our bodies, which death into dust reduced, to their souls again be joined, that so to the whole man it be well or ill, according as well or ill he acted.

But moreover the greatest divinity indication in sacred Scripture is its efficacy, by which inwardly in the man it acts, partly indeed by terrifying consciences, and with sin's sense affecting, partly by raising the bruised mind and afflicted consciences consoling: But chiefly so the man changing, that sin he hate, and piety and true virtue from the soul pursue: by which efficacy indeed nothing more powerful is in the faithful confirming, although to assent it cannot compel those who not yet that efficacy have felt, and against God's Word have hardened. And yet a man most profane, even if God's Word's efficacy he has not felt, if yet that attentively he considers, easily can recognize this Word such to be, that highest tranquillity and joy it generates in those who to it firmly believe, and them to every good work and every virtue compels.

And these few things may suffice to have tasted of this argument which never can be exhausted, and which more fully and copiously is treated by learned men, whose footsteps we follow, and who to us the torch have borne before. But this seems to be added, namely these divinity characters, which in Scripture to shine we said, are not to be sought in single Scripture parts from the whole separated, but in the divine writings as they are considered jointly, and according to themselves as wholes. For nor is it to be thought that any Canonical book's pericope has a certain mark by which it can from the Apocrypha be discerned and distinguished.
pass_b_english:
Sacred Scripture's precepts and dogmas also do not lack their own light — nay, they have by far the greatest. That this may appear more clearly, note that they are of two kinds. For Scripture teaches and commands many things of which men have by nature some notice, but very confused and wavering. Yet Scripture has laid those things open more lucidly, and taught them fully and accurately. Of this sort are what Scripture hands down concerning God's nature and attributes — namely concerning God's eternal, immense, and immutable essence; concerning his infinite power, wisdom, goodness, and also justice; concerning the creation of the world and of all that is in it; concerning God's providence by which he conserves, rules, and administers all things; likewise concerning man's office both toward God and toward the neighbor: that God is to be loved above all, all things referred to his glory, himself carefully worshiped and invoked, trusted, and that one is to rest upon his care; that the neighbor also is to be loved, good done to all, injuries borne, oneself thought of humbly, innermost thoughts and affections kept pure — and in a word, nearly all and each of the precepts of the Christian life, which ought to be pure and sincere in every part, and from which all filth and luxury ought to be absent. Those things and the like the sense of conscience proves, reason confirms, and certain rudiments of them are discerned in the pagans' books. For they hand down some things concerning God, piety, and man's office that are not contemptible — yet obscurely, sparingly, coldly, doubtfully, and mixed with very many errors. But Scripture places those things in clear light and teaches them fully and openly: so that after its light has shone on us, we wonder that things so certain and undoubted were seen and handed down only thinly, doubtfully, and obscurely by the most excellent minds. But when those most excellent minds handed down so jejunely and obscurely the things whose truth we now discern by Scripture's benefit, while Scripture handed them down so fully and perspicuously — and yet the sacred writers did not excel other men by erudition or by nature's gifts, but on the contrary most were rude and unlearned in the human sciences — it is necessary that they were led by another light than nature's, and taught and inspired by God.

But besides those things of which men have by nature only a thin and fleeing cognition, sacred Scripture teaches many things that surpass reason, which the human mind cannot grasp, and for which it has no certain arguments. Yet they cohere so well with what the sense of conscience proves and right reason is convinced of, and agree so well with those prior things, and are built upon them so fittingly, that it sufficiently appears they are not human inventions but mysteries of divine wisdom. Such, for example, is the doctrine of the expiation of our sins through the death and offering on the cross of Christ, God and man — which is discerned to agree most with God's justice and mercy. For in this manner God's justice was satisfied while our sins were punished in Christ, and mercy while they were forgiven us. And with this doctrine coheres that dogma so sublime and lofty concerning three divine persons in one essence. For unless the Son of God were God and equal to the Father, his sacrifice would not have been of infinite value, such as was required that by it our sins be expiated, inasmuch as they had deserved infinite punishment. And such also is the doctrine of the resurrection of the dead. For it seems agreeable to reason that a man who acts well or ill in the body should also receive in the body punishment or reward for what was done justly or unjustly — which, since it does not happen in this life, agrees with God's justice that our bodies, which death has reduced to dust, be joined again to their souls, so that it may go well or ill with the whole man according as he acted well or ill.

But moreover the greatest indication of divinity in sacred Scripture is its efficacy, by which it acts inwardly in a man — partly by terrifying consciences and affecting them with the sense of sin, partly by raising the bruised mind and consoling afflicted consciences; but chiefly by so changing the man that he hates sin and pursues piety and true virtue from the soul. By this efficacy nothing is more powerful in confirming the faithful, although it cannot compel to assent those who have not yet felt that efficacy and have hardened against God's Word. And yet even a most profane man, if he has not felt the efficacy of God's Word, yet if he considers it attentively, can easily recognize that this Word is such as to generate the highest tranquillity and joy in those who firmly believe it, and to compel them to every good work and every virtue.

And let these few things suffice as a taste of this argument, which can never be exhausted, and which is treated more fully and copiously by learned men whose footsteps we follow and who have borne the torch before us. But this seems worth adding: that these characters of divinity which we said shine in Scripture are not to be sought in single parts of Scripture separated from the whole, but in the divine writings as they are considered jointly and as wholes in themselves. For it is not to be thought that any pericope of a Canonical book has a certain mark by which it can be discerned and distinguished from the Apocrypha.
source_text:
XLIII. Sua quoque luce non carent, imo multo maximam habent, Scripturae sacrae praecepta et dogmata. Quod ut clarius appareat, notandum est illa duorum esse generum. Multa enim docet et jubet Scriptura quorum homines per naturam notitiam aliquam habent, sed confusam valde atque vacillantem. Verum Scriptura ista luculentius patefecit, et docuit plene atque accurate. Ejusmodi sunt quae Scriptura tradit de Dei natura atque attributis, nempe de Dei essentia aeterna, immensa, et immutabili, et de infinita illius potentia, sapientia, bonitate, atque etiam justitia, de creatione mundi et omnium quae in eo sunt, de providentia Dei qua cuncta conservat, regit, et administrat: Item de hominis officio tam erga Deum, quam erga proximum, qualia sunt esse Deum supra omnia amandum, omnia in ipsius gloriam referenda, ipsum esse sedulo colendum atque invocandum, ipsi fidendum, et in curam illius recumbendum esse. Proximum quoque esse diligendum, omnibus benefaciendum, ferendas esse injurias, humiliter de se sentiendum esse, cogitationes et affectus intimos puros esse servandos, et uno verbo, omnia et singula fere praecepta vitae Christianae, quae omni ex parte pura et sincera esse debet, et a qua debet abesse spurcitia et luxuria omnis. Illa certe et similia probat conscientiae sensus, confirmat ratio, et eorum quaedam rudimenta cernuntur in Ethnicorum libris. Etenim nonnulla de Deo, de pietate atque hominis officio non contemnenda tradunt. Sed tamen obscure, parce, frigide, dubitanter, atque cum plurimorum errorum admixtione. Scriptura vero ista in clara luce ponit, pleneque et aperte docet: ita ut postquam nobis lux illius splenduit, miremur res tam certas atque indubitatas nonnisi tenuiter, dubitanter et obscure a praestantissimis ingeniis perspectas traditasque fuisse. Cum autem ingenia illa praestantissima, res illas, quarum jam veritatem cernimus Scripturae beneficio, ita jejune et obscure tradiderint, Scriptura vero ita plene et perspicue; neque tamen Scriptores sacri eruditione, aut naturae dotibus supra caeteros homines praecelluerint, imo contra fuerint plerique scientiarum humanarum rudes et idiotae, necesse est illos alio quam naturae lumine ductos esse, atque a Deo doctos et inspiratos.

XLIV. Sed praeter ista, quorum homines per naturam tenuem quandam, atque fugientem cognitionem habent, Scriptura sacra multa docet quae rationem superant, neque mens humana illa capere potest, nec eorum habet certa argumenta: Verumtamen tam bene cohaerent cum iis quae probat conscientiae sensus, et de quibus recta ratio convincitur, et prioribus illis tam consentanea sunt, et ita congruenter et apposite superstructa, ut satis appareat non esse commenta humana, sed sapientiae divinae mysteria. Talis est ex. gr. doctrina de peccatorum nostrorum expiatione per Christi Dei et hominis mortem et oblationem in cruce factam, quae congruere maxime cernitur cum Dei justitia et misericordia. Hoc enim modo justitiae Dei satisfactum est, dum peccata nostra in Christo punita sunt, et misericordiae, dum nobis condonata. Et cum hac doctrina cohaeret dogma illud tam sublime et excelsum de tribus personis divinis in una essentia. Nam nisi Dei filius Deus esset, et aequalis patri, sacrificium ejus non fuisset valoris infiniti, quale requirebatur, ut eo peccata nostra expiarentur, quandoquidem infinitam poenam promeruerant. Et talis quoque doctrina de mortuorum resurrectione. Videtur enim esse rationi consentaneum, ut homo qui in corpore bene vel male agit, in corpore quoque poenam, vel mercedem accipiat juste vel injuste factorum: quod cum in hac vita non fiat, justitiae Dei congruit, ut corpora nostra, quae mors in pulverem redegit, animabus suis denuo jungantur, ut ita homini integro, vel bene, vel male sit, prout bene, vel male egerit.

XLV. Sed praeterea maximum divinitatis indicium in Scriptura sacra est ejus efficacia, qua intus in homine agit, partim quidem terrendo conscientias, et peccati sensu afficiendo, partim erigendo animum attritum et conscientias afflictas consolando: Sed praecipue ita hominem immutando, ut peccatum odio habeat, et pietatem veramque virtutem ex animo sectetur: qua quidem efficacia nihil potentius est in fidelibus confirmandis, licet ad assensum compellere non possit eos, qui nondum istam efficaciam senserunt, et adversus Dei verbum obduruerunt. Et tamen homo maxime profanus, etiamsi verbi Dei efficaciam non senserit, si tamen illud attente consideret, facile potest agnoscere hoc verbum tale esse, ut summam tranquillitatem et gaudium generet in iis qui illi firmiter credunt, eosque ad omne bonum opus et omnem virtutem compellat.

XLVI. Atque haec pauca sufficiat delibasse de hoc argumento quod nunquam exhauriri potest, quodque fusius et copiosius tractatur a viris doctis, quorum vestigia sequimur, et qui nobis facem praetulerunt. Hoc autem addendum videtur, nempe characteres hosce divinitatis, quos in Scriptura fulgere diximus, non esse quaerendos in singulis Scripturae partibus a toto separatis, sed in scriptis divinis prout considerantur conjunctim, et secundum se tota. Nec enim putandum est quamvis Canonici libri pericopen, certam habere notam, qua possit ab Apocrypha discerni et distingui.
